title: American Sign Language
description: An introduction to American Sign Language covering fingerspelling, core vocabulary, and the grammar that makes ASL a full, independent language distinct from English, including facial grammar, topic-comment sentence structure, and the use of space to reference people and things. You will also learn foundational Deaf culture and etiquette so you can communicate respectfully as well as accurately.
outcomes: You can fingerspell the English alphabet and read back basic fingerspelled words.
You can sign basic greetings, introductions, and numbers 1-10.
You can form yes/no and WH-questions using the correct facial grammar (non-manual signals).
You can build simple ASL sentences using topic-comment order instead of English word order.
You can use space and pronouns to refer to people and things established earlier in a conversation.
You can describe key Deaf cultural norms and etiquette, including how to get someone's attention appropriately.

units.title: Getting Started: ASL and Deaf Culture
units.summary: Before learning signs, this unit establishes what ASL actually is, the cultural norms that come with it, and the manual alphabet used for fingerspelling.

lessons.title: What Is ASL? A Language, Not Coded English
lessons.intro: American Sign Language is not English translated into gestures, and not a universal sign language shared by all Deaf people worldwide — it is its own complete, natural language, with its own grammar, that happens to have developed in the United States and parts of Canada.

sections.heading: A Language With Its Own Grammar
body: ASL has a grammar entirely independent of English: it typically orders sentences by topic first and comment second rather than English's subject-verb-object order, it shows grammatical information like questions and negation through facial expression and head movement, and it uses the physical space in front of the signer to track who and what is being talked about. None of these features are borrowed from English — they evolved as ASL's own solutions to the demands of a visual-manual language.

Because ASL is not a manual code for English, word-for-word signing of an English sentence (sometimes called Signed Exact English, a separate manual system) looks and functions differently from natural ASL. A fluent ASL sentence describing 'I gave the book to my sister yesterday' might place time first, establish 'sister' and 'book' spatially, and use a directional verb that moves toward the established location for 'sister' — all without a sign-for-sign match to the English word order.

sections.heading: One Language Among Many Sign Languages
body: ASL is historically related to French Sign Language (LSF), following from the founding of the first American school for deaf students in 1817 by Laurent Clerc, a Deaf French educator, and Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet. As a result, ASL and LSF share a meaningful amount of vocabulary today, even though ASL has evolved independently for two centuries since.

Sign languages are not mutually intelligible across countries any more than spoken languages are: British Sign Language (BSL), for instance, is not simply English on the hands either, and is in fact largely unintelligible to ASL signers despite both countries speaking English — strong evidence that a sign language's grammar and vocabulary are shaped by its Deaf community's history, not by the surrounding spoken language.

example.problem: Explain why an ASL signer and a BSL signer, both fluent in their own sign language, would likely struggle to understand each other even though English speakers in both countries can understand one another.
steps: Sign languages are independent languages, not visual codes for the spoken language around them.
ASL descends historically from French Sign Language (LSF), while BSL developed through a separate lineage in Britain.
Because their grammars and vocabularies developed independently, mutual intelligibility between ASL and BSL is low, unlike the shared intelligibility of American and British English.
example.answer: ASL and BSL are historically and grammatically distinct languages — ASL relates to French Sign Language, not British Sign Language — so fluency in one does not transfer to the other, unlike spoken American and British English.

keyTerms.def: A complete, natural language with its own grammar, used primarily by Deaf communities in the United States and parts of Canada.
ASL's typical sentence pattern, establishing what is being discussed (topic) before stating information about it (comment).
A manually coded system representing English word-for-word, distinct from and not equivalent to natural ASL.

practice.q: Is ASL a manual version of English?
choices: No — it is an independent language with its own grammar
Yes — it signs English word for word
Yes, but only for questions
No — it is a universal sign language used worldwide
practice.explain: ASL has its own grammar (topic-comment order, facial grammar, spatial reference) independent of English; signing English word-for-word is a separate system called Signed Exact English.

practice.q: Which language is ASL historically related to?
choices: French Sign Language (LSF)
British Sign Language (BSL)
Spoken French
Spoken English
practice.explain: ASL developed from a blend that included French Sign Language, brought to the U.S. by Laurent Clerc in the founding of the first American deaf school in 1817.

practice.q: Why can't an ASL signer generally understand a BSL signer, even though both countries speak English?
choices: ASL and BSL are separate languages with independent histories and grammars
BSL is simply a slower version of ASL
ASL signers refuse to learn BSL out of preference
Sign languages are always identical to the spoken language of their country
practice.explain: Sign languages develop independently of surrounding spoken languages; ASL's lineage traces to French Sign Language, not British Sign Language, so the two are not mutually intelligible.

lessons.title: Deaf Culture and Etiquette
lessons.intro: Learning signs without learning Deaf cultural norms is like learning vocabulary in a spoken language without ever learning how to be polite — technically communicating, but missing the practical rules that make you welcome in the community.

sections.heading: Deaf With a Capital D
body: Many members of the Deaf community distinguish between 'deaf' (lowercase, describing the audiological condition of not hearing) and 'Deaf' (capitalized, describing cultural identity and membership in a community that shares ASL, values, and traditions). Not every person with hearing loss identifies as culturally Deaf, and not every culturally Deaf person has zero hearing — the distinction is about community and identity, not solely about a hearing test result.

It is also considered important to avoid the term 'hearing-impaired,' which frames deafness as a deficiency relative to a hearing-centered norm; 'deaf' and 'hard of hearing' are the terms generally preferred by the community itself. Following the community's own preferred terminology is one of the simplest and most respected signs of a considerate learner.

sections.heading: Getting Attention and Basic Etiquette
body: Because ASL is a visual language, getting someone's attention appropriately matters: acceptable methods include a light tap on the shoulder or arm, waving a hand gently in someone's peripheral vision, or flicking a light switch once in a room (never done abruptly or repeatedly, which can come across as alarming). Shouting a Deaf person's name or grabbing them suddenly are both considered rude, since neither respects how a Deaf person actually perceives the environment.

During a conversation, maintaining eye contact is expected and important — looking away frequently can seem disengaged or rude, unlike in some hearing conversational norms where occasional eye contact is sufficient. If you need to temporarily break attention (to write something down, for instance), briefly touching the other person's arm or hand first signals that you are not ending the conversation, only pausing it.

keyTerms.def: Describes cultural identity and membership in a community sharing ASL and Deaf traditions, as distinct from lowercase 'deaf,' an audiological description.
A preferred term for partial hearing loss; 'hearing-impaired' is generally avoided as it frames deafness as a deficiency.
Using a light tap, a gentle wave in the visual field, or a single light flick — never shouting or sudden grabbing.

practice.q: What is the key difference between 'deaf' and 'Deaf' as commonly used in the community?
choices: Capital-D Deaf refers to cultural identity and community; lowercase deaf refers to audiological status
There is no difference; capitalization is random
Deaf refers only to people born without hearing
Deaf is an outdated term no longer used
practice.explain: The community distinguishes cultural/community identity (Deaf) from the medical/audiological fact of hearing loss (deaf).

practice.q: Which term does the Deaf community generally prefer to avoid?
choices: Hearing-impaired
Deaf
Hard of hearing
ASL user
practice.explain: 'Hearing-impaired' frames deafness relative to a hearing norm as a deficiency, and is generally avoided in favor of 'deaf' or 'hard of hearing.'

practice.q: What is an appropriate way to get a Deaf person's attention from a short distance?
choices: A gentle wave within their field of vision
Shouting their name loudly
Grabbing their arm suddenly
Standing behind them and clapping
practice.explain: Gentle, visible signals (a wave, a light tap, a light flick) respect how a Deaf person perceives their environment; shouting or grabbing does not.

lessons.title: The Manual Alphabet: Fingerspelling
lessons.intro: Fingerspelling lets you represent any English word letter by letter using one hand, and it is indispensable for names, places, and technical terms that do not have an established sign, but it is meant to be used sparingly and read as whole word-shapes, not letter by letter.

sections.heading: How the Manual Alphabet Works
body: The ASL manual alphabet uses 26 distinct handshapes, one per English letter, signed with the dominant hand held roughly at chest height, palm generally facing outward toward the person you are addressing. Several letters are visually similar and distinguished mainly by small differences in finger position: for example, the letters M and N are both made with the thumb tucked under folded fingers, differing only in how many fingers are folded over the thumb (three for M, two for N).

A few letters involve movement rather than a single static shape: J is signed by tracing the shape of the letter J in the air with the pinky finger extended, and Z is signed by tracing a Z shape in the air with the index finger extended. Every other letter of the alphabet is a held, static handshape with no movement.

sections.heading: Reading and Producing Fingerspelling Well
body: Fluent fingerspelling is read as a whole word-shape rather than letter by letter, the same way a fluent reader recognizes 'the' as a shape rather than sounding out t-h-e — this is why beginners can produce letters correctly but still struggle to read fingerspelling at a natural conversational speed, since reading fingerspelling is a distinct skill from producing it. Slowing down your own fingerspelling smoothly, rather than pausing awkwardly between letters, is more readable to a fluent signer than either rushing or over-separating each letter.

In natural ASL conversation, fingerspelling is reserved mainly for proper names, brand names, technical vocabulary without an established sign, and occasionally short common words for emphasis. Overusing fingerspelling in place of established signs — spelling out words that already have a perfectly good sign — is a common beginner habit that fluent signers can immediately spot as inexperience.

example.problem: You need to fingerspell your name, 'AMY,' to someone for the first time. What handshape movement pattern should you use, and how should you pace it?
steps: Sign A, M, and Y as static handshapes (none of these three letters involve air-traced movement).
Hold the dominant hand steady at chest height, palm generally facing the other person.
Move smoothly and evenly from one letter to the next rather than pausing sharply between each shape, since a smooth, steady pace is easier for a fluent reader to follow than a rushed or choppy one.
example.answer: Fingerspell A-M-Y as three static handshapes at chest height, transitioning smoothly and at a steady, moderate pace rather than rushing or freezing between letters.

keyTerms.def: The set of 26 handshapes representing the English letters A-Z, used for fingerspelling.
Spelling a word letter by letter using the manual alphabet, used mainly for names and words without an established sign.
Reading fingerspelling by recognizing the overall shape/rhythm of a familiar word rather than parsing each letter individually.

practice.q: Which two letters of the manual alphabet involve tracing movement in the air rather than a static handshape?
choices: J and Z
M and N
A and B
All 26 letters involve movement
practice.explain: J and Z are traced in the air (J with the pinky, Z with the index finger); every other letter is a held static shape.

practice.q: Why might a beginner produce fingerspelled letters accurately but still struggle to read fingerspelling from a fluent signer?
choices: Fluent signers read fingerspelling as whole word-shapes, a different skill from producing individual letters
Fluent signers use a completely different alphabet when reading
Reading fingerspelling requires no practice at all
Fingerspelling is read from right to left instead of left to right
practice.explain: Producing letters correctly and reading fluent, word-shape-paced fingerspelling are distinct skills, which is why reading takes separate practice.

practice.q: When is fingerspelling most appropriate in natural ASL conversation?
choices: For proper names and words without an established ASL sign
For every single word in a sentence
Only for numbers
Never — fingerspelling is considered incorrect ASL
practice.explain: Fingerspelling is reserved mainly for names, brands, and technical terms lacking a sign; overusing it in place of established signs marks inexperience.

units.title: Basic Conversation
units.summary: This unit builds the first real conversational toolkit: greetings, introductions, numbers, and the two basic question types every conversation needs.

lessons.title: Greetings and Introductions
lessons.intro: Every conversation in ASL, just as in any language, starts with the same handful of moves — a greeting, a name exchange, and a question about how someone is — and getting comfortable with these first exchanges builds the confidence to keep going.

sections.heading: Hello and How Are You
body: The sign for HELLO is typically made with a flat hand near the forehead moving outward and slightly down, similar in feel to a small salute, and it can be used at any time of day, unlike English's time-specific 'good morning' or 'good evening.' Following a greeting, the sign for HOW-ARE-YOU combines the sign for the question word HOW with a facial expression of genuine inquiry — raised eyebrows and a slightly tilted head — which is not optional decoration but a required grammatical part of forming a question, covered fully in Unit 3.

A common response is FINE (or GOOD), often a flat hand moving from the chest outward, paired with a small nod. Just as in Hawaiian and many other languages, it is polite to return the question with a sign roughly meaning 'and you?', typically formed by pointing toward the other person with raised eyebrows, letting the facial expression alone carry the question.

sections.heading: Introducing Yourself
body: To introduce yourself, sign NAME (commonly, the middle and index fingers of one hand tapping the same fingers of the other hand, twice) followed by a point to yourself (MY) and then your name fingerspelled or, if you have one, your established name sign. A first introduction might follow the pattern: NAME MY [fingerspelled name], asking the other person's name in return with NAME YOUR-WHAT (a question sign combining NAME with a WH-question facial expression).

A name sign is a unique sign representing a specific person, usually assigned within the Deaf community rather than self-chosen by a hearing learner, and often incorporates a handshape related to the person's initial along with a location or movement tied to a personal characteristic. Until a learner is given one by a Deaf community member, fingerspelling your name in full is the standard, respectful approach.

example.problem: You meet someone for the first time. Describe, in order, the sequence of signs and facial expressions for a complete first greeting and introduction exchange.
steps: Sign HELLO to open the interaction.
Sign HOW-ARE-YOU with raised eyebrows and an inquiring facial expression, since the expression is required grammar, not optional.
Respond or wait for a response such as FINE, then return the question with a point plus raised eyebrows ('and you?').
Introduce yourself: NAME MY, followed by your fingerspelled name.
Ask their name in return: NAME YOUR-WHAT, with the appropriate WH-question facial expression.
example.answer: HELLO -> HOW-ARE-YOU (eyebrows raised) -> FINE, and-you? -> NAME MY [fingerspelled name] -> NAME YOUR-WHAT?

keyTerms.def: A unique ASL sign representing a specific person, typically given by the Deaf community rather than self-assigned.
A greeting question requiring both the manual sign and a required facial expression of inquiry.

practice.q: Why is the raised-eyebrow facial expression during HOW-ARE-YOU not optional?
choices: It is a required grammatical marker of a question in ASL, not just decoration
It only matters for very formal conversations
It is a regional style choice with no grammatical meaning
It only applies to yes/no questions, not this greeting
practice.explain: Facial expression carries essential grammatical information in ASL questions; without it, the sentence isn't grammatically marked as a question.

practice.q: What is a 'name sign,' and how should a new learner typically handle introducing their own name?
choices: A unique sign usually given by the Deaf community; until then, fingerspell your name in full
Any sign a learner invents for themselves on day one
A sign that is identical for everyone with the same first letter
A formal legal requirement processed through paperwork
practice.explain: Name signs are typically assigned within the Deaf community; a respectful default before receiving one is fingerspelling your full name.

practice.q: What does the sign pattern NAME MY typically introduce?
choices: The signer's own name
A question asking someone else's name
A greeting meaning 'nice to meet you'
A farewell phrase
practice.explain: NAME MY, followed by the fingerspelled or sign name, is the standard pattern for stating your own name.

lessons.title: Numbers 1-10 and Age
lessons.intro: Numbers are some of the most frequently used signs in daily life — prices, ages, phone numbers, times — and ASL numbers 1 through 10 each use a distinct, memorable handshape that becomes automatic with a little repetition.

sections.heading: Counting One Through Five
body: Numbers 1 through 4 in ASL are signed by extending that many fingers starting from the index finger (1: index finger only; 2: index and middle; 3: index, middle, and ring; 4: index through pinky, thumb tucked in), palm generally facing outward. The number 5 extends all five fingers, including the thumb, spread naturally apart.

Unlike counting on fingers casually in English, which often starts with the thumb, ASL numeral handshapes are standardized and consistent — learning them precisely, rather than approximating with casual finger-counting habits from English, prevents confusion, since an ASL numeral is a specific linguistic sign, not a loose gesture.

sections.heading: Six Through Ten and Asking Age
body: Numbers 6 through 9 introduce the thumb touching a specific finger while the remaining fingers stay extended: 6 touches the thumb to the pinky, 7 touches the thumb to the ring finger, 8 touches the thumb to the middle finger, and 9 touches the thumb to the index finger, with the other fingers extended in each case. The number 10 is signed with a closed fist, thumb extended upward, shaking slightly side to side.

To ask someone's age, sign HOW-OLD (or AGE) combined with a WH-question facial expression (furrowed eyebrows, slightly forward head tilt), and answer with just the number: a question like HOW-OLD YOU might be answered simply with the number sign 7, since ASL frequently drops words English would require, such as 'years old,' once age is the established topic.

example.problem: How would you sign 'I am 7 years old' in a natural ASL structure, keeping in mind ASL often omits words English requires?
steps: ASL frequently drops 'years old' as redundant once age is established as the topic.
Sign the pronoun/point to self (I/ME).
Sign the number 7, formed with the thumb touching the ring finger, remaining fingers extended.
example.answer: ME 7 (the number 7 alone conveys 'years old' once age is the established topic).

keyTerms.def: Standardized finger-count shapes for 1 through 5, extending fingers from the index outward, all five for 5.
6-9 combine the thumb touching a specific finger with the rest extended; 10 is a fist with thumb extended, shaking slightly.
The question sign for age, requiring a WH-question facial expression; answers are often just the number.

practice.q: How is the ASL number 8 formed?
choices: Thumb touching the middle finger, remaining fingers extended
All five fingers extended and spread
Thumb touching the pinky finger
A closed fist with no fingers extended
practice.explain: 8 is signed with the thumb touching the middle finger while the index, ring, and pinky stay extended.

practice.q: How does ASL typically answer 'How old are you?' when the topic of age is already established?
choices: With just the number, often omitting a separate sign for 'years old'
By fingerspelling the entire phrase 'years old'
By repeating the question back unanswered
By using the number 10 to mean 'old enough'
practice.explain: Once AGE/HOW-OLD sets the topic, ASL frequently answers with the bare number, since 'years old' becomes redundant information.

practice.q: What is different about ASL numeral handshapes compared to casual English finger-counting?
choices: ASL numerals are standardized, specific linguistic signs, not loose approximations
ASL has no numbers below 5
English finger-counting and ASL numerals are identical in every region
ASL numbers change meaning depending on which hand is used
practice.explain: ASL numeral handshapes are fixed, standardized signs, unlike casual, inconsistent finger-counting habits some hearing people use.

lessons.title: Yes/No and WH-Questions
lessons.intro: In spoken English a question is often marked by rearranging words or raising your voice at the end of a sentence — in ASL, the question is marked almost entirely on your face and the tilt of your head, which is why facial grammar cannot be treated as optional.

sections.heading: Yes/No Questions
body: A yes/no question in ASL — one answerable simply with yes or no — is marked by raised eyebrows, widened eyes, and often a slight forward head or body tilt held through the entire question, with the manual signs otherwise staying close to statement word order. YOU HUNGRY, signed with this facial marking, means 'Are you hungry?'; the exact same manual signs without the facial marking would instead read as a flat statement, 'You are hungry.'

Because the non-manual signal, not a rearranged sentence, is what marks the question, dropping the facial expression is a genuine grammar error in ASL — comparable to a spoken English speaker leaving out a question mark's rising intonation and expecting to still be understood as asking something. Beginners often under-use facial expression because it feels exaggerated at first, but under-marking a question changes its meaning, not just its style.

sections.heading: WH-Questions
body: WH-questions — those built around question words like WHO, WHAT, WHERE, WHEN, WHY, and HOW — use a different facial marker: furrowed, lowered eyebrows (rather than the raised eyebrows of yes/no questions), often with a slight head tilt or forward lean, held for the duration of the question. The question word itself commonly appears at the end of the ASL sentence, a notable difference from English, which places it first: YOU NAME WHAT? ('What is your name?')

The question word can also appear at the beginning or even in both positions for emphasis in some registers, but placing it at the sentence's end is extremely common in natural, unscripted ASL and is often the first pattern taught to new learners because it clearly demonstrates the topic-comment order covered fully in the next unit — establish the topic (YOU NAME) before asking the actual question (WHAT).

example.problem: Contrast how you would sign 'You are going home' versus 'Are you going home?' versus 'Where are you going?'
steps: Statement: YOU GO HOME, signed with a neutral, non-question facial expression.
Yes/no question: YOU GO HOME, with raised eyebrows and a forward head tilt held through the sentence, the same signs but a different face.
WH-question: YOU GO WHERE, with furrowed eyebrows and the question word WHERE placed at the end.
example.answer: YOU GO HOME (neutral face, statement); YOU GO HOME (eyebrows raised, yes/no question); YOU GO WHERE (eyebrows furrowed, WH-question).

keyTerms.def: Grammatical information carried by facial expression, head tilt, or body posture rather than the hands.
Raised eyebrows, widened eyes, and a forward head/body tilt held through a yes/no question.
Furrowed, lowered eyebrows, often with a head tilt, held through a question built on a WH-word; the WH-word often appears sentence-finally.

practice.q: What single change turns the ASL statement YOU HUNGRY into the question 'Are you hungry?'
choices: Adding raised eyebrows and a forward head tilt held through the signs
Reversing the order of the two signs
Adding the sign for 'question' before HUNGRY
Signing it more slowly
practice.explain: The manual signs can stay the same; the required non-manual signal (raised eyebrows, forward tilt) is what marks it as a yes/no question.

practice.q: Where does the WH-word commonly appear in a natural ASL WH-question, such as 'What is your name?'
choices: Often at the end of the sentence, e.g. YOU NAME WHAT
Always at the very beginning, e.g. WHAT YOU NAME
In the exact middle of the sentence only
WH-words are never signed at all
practice.explain: Placing the WH-word at the sentence's end (YOU NAME WHAT?) is a very common natural ASL pattern, differing from English's WH-word-first order.

practice.q: What facial expression distinguishes a WH-question from a yes/no question in ASL?
choices: Furrowed, lowered eyebrows for WH-questions versus raised eyebrows for yes/no questions
There is no facial difference between the two question types
WH-questions require a smile, yes/no questions require a frown
Only yes/no questions require any facial marking
practice.explain: WH-questions use furrowed/lowered eyebrows, while yes/no questions use raised eyebrows — the two non-manual markers are distinct and both grammatically required.

units.title: ASL Grammar Foundations
units.summary: This unit builds the core grammatical machinery of ASL: facial grammar beyond questions, topic-comment sentence order, and the spatial system behind pronouns.

lessons.title: Non-Manual Signals: Grammar on the Face
lessons.intro: You have already met three non-manual signals — for yes/no questions, WH-questions, and general inquiry — but facial grammar in ASL extends far beyond questions, marking negation, conditionals, and even how intensely something is described.

sections.heading: Negation on the Face
body: A head shake — moving the head side to side, similar to the English gesture for 'no' — accompanies a negated ASL sentence and can, in some constructions, be the primary or only marker of negation, layered over signs that would otherwise read as a positive statement. ME LIKE COFFEE, signed with a head shake through the sentence, can mean 'I don't like coffee,' even without a separate manual sign for 'not' in some phrasings, similar to how eyebrow position marks questions without changing the underlying words.

More commonly, a manual negation sign (such as NOT or NONE, depending on context) is combined with the head shake for clarity, especially in careful or formal registers: ME NOT LIKE COFFEE, with a head shake accompanying NOT and continuing through LIKE COFFEE. Dropping the head shake while still using a manual NOT sign is a common, noticeable error for beginning signers.

sections.heading: Intensity, Conditionals, and Topic Marking
body: Facial intensity — wide eyes, pursed lips, puffed cheeks, or other exaggerated expressions — can function grammatically like an adverb, showing degree without an extra manual sign: a sign for BIG made with widened eyes and a slightly open mouth can mean 'huge' or 'enormous,' intensifying the base sign purely through the face. This is one reason ASL is often described as visually expressive by hearing observers — the expressiveness is frequently doing real grammatical work, not just conveying emotion.

Conditional sentences ('if... then...') use a distinct non-manual marker too: raised eyebrows and a slight pause or head tilt mark the 'if' clause, often before the sign IF itself, then the face relaxes for the 'then' result clause. Topic marking, covered fully in the next lesson, uses yet another distinct signal — raised eyebrows with a brief pause — to set apart the topic of a sentence before the comment about it begins.

example.problem: How would a signer show 'I am NOT going,' relying on facial grammar as the primary tool, with or without an extra manual sign for emphasis?
steps: Sign ME GO.
Add a head shake over the sentence to mark negation, which can on its own convey 'not.'
Optionally add the manual sign NOT before or during GO for extra clarity, still paired with the head shake.
example.answer: ME GO with a head shake (basic negation), or ME NOT GO with the head shake continuing through the sentence for added clarity.

keyTerms.def: A side-to-side head movement marking negation, which can function as the primary or only marker of 'not.'
Exaggerated facial expression (wide eyes, pursed lips) that grammatically intensifies a sign's degree, like an adverb.
Raised eyebrows and a head tilt marking an 'if' clause, relaxing for the 'then' result clause.

practice.q: What does a head shake accompanying a signed sentence typically mark?
choices: Negation ('not')
A question
Intensity or exaggeration
Past tense
practice.explain: A side-to-side head shake is the standard non-manual marker of negation in ASL, sometimes functioning alone without a separate manual 'not' sign.

practice.q: How can a signer show that something is 'huge' rather than just 'big' without adding a new manual sign?
choices: Widen the eyes and intensify the facial expression while signing BIG
Sign BIG twice in a row
Add a head shake
Fingerspell H-U-G-E instead
practice.explain: Facial intensity functions grammatically like an intensifying adverb, changing BIG's meaning toward 'huge' through expression alone.

practice.q: What non-manual signal marks the 'if' clause of a conditional sentence?
choices: Raised eyebrows and a head tilt, relaxing for the result clause
A head shake throughout the entire sentence
Furrowed eyebrows only, identical to a WH-question
Puffed cheeks with no eyebrow movement
practice.explain: Conditional 'if' clauses use raised eyebrows and a head tilt, distinct from the head shake of negation or the furrowed brow of WH-questions.

lessons.title: Topic-Comment Sentence Structure
lessons.intro: English almost always states the subject before anything else, but ASL frequently flips this by naming the topic — what the sentence is about — first, then commenting on it, a structural difference that changes how you should think about building sentences from scratch.

sections.heading: What Topic-Comment Order Looks Like
body: In topic-comment structure, the signer first establishes what the sentence is about (the topic), marked with raised eyebrows and a brief pause, and then signs new information about that topic (the comment), typically with a neutral or falling facial expression. The English sentence 'I already ate the pizza' might become PIZZA, ME EAT FINISH in ASL — PIZZA is raised as the topic first, then ME EAT FINISH comments on it, with FINISH marking that the eating is already completed.

This differs from simply moving an object to the front of an English sentence for emphasis ('Pizza, I already ate') because in ASL the topic-marking eyebrow raise and pause are a required grammatical signal, not an optional stylistic choice — omitting the non-manual marker while still fronting PIZZA would leave the sentence structurally incomplete or ambiguous rather than merely less emphatic.

sections.heading: When to Use Topic-Comment Versus Simple Order
body: Not every ASL sentence needs an explicit topic-comment structure — short, simple sentences with a clear, already-obvious subject, like ME HUNGRY, are perfectly natural without fronting anything as a marked topic. Topic-comment order becomes especially useful when introducing a new subject into a conversation, contrasting two things, or referring back to something already established earlier, since fronting the topic tells your conversation partner exactly what new information is about to follow.

A signer discussing two different people's food preferences might use topic-comment structure specifically to keep the contrast clear: COFFEE, ME LIKE. TEA, ME NOT-LIKE — fronting COFFEE and then TEA as separate topics makes the contrast between the two comments unambiguous in a way that a single run-on sentence would not.

example.problem: Using topic-comment structure, express 'My sister already finished her homework' where SISTER, HOMEWORK, FINISH, and MY (a point to self) are the available signs.
steps: Establish the topic: SISTER (with raised eyebrows and a brief pause, marking her as what the sentence is about).
Comment on the topic with the remaining information: HOMEWORK FINISH, using FINISH to show the action is already completed.
example.answer: SISTER, HOMEWORK FINISH (topic: sister, marked with raised eyebrows and a pause; comment: her homework is finished).

keyTerms.def: An ASL sentence pattern establishing the topic first (marked with raised eyebrows and a pause), then commenting on it.
A sign used to show that an action has already been completed, functioning like English's past perfect.

practice.q: What non-manual signal marks a topic at the front of an ASL sentence?
choices: Raised eyebrows and a brief pause
A head shake
Furrowed eyebrows held through the whole sentence
No facial signal is needed if the sign is fronted
practice.explain: Topic marking requires raised eyebrows and a pause after the fronted sign; without it, the sentence isn't grammatically marked as topic-comment.

practice.q: In PIZZA, ME EAT FINISH, what grammatical information does FINISH add?
choices: That the eating is already completed
That pizza is the direct object
That the sentence is a question
That the speaker dislikes pizza
practice.explain: FINISH functions as an aspect marker showing the action is already completed, similar to English 'already ate.'

practice.q: When is topic-comment structure especially useful compared to simple sentence order?
choices: When introducing a new subject, contrasting two things, or referring back to something already established
Only when asking a yes/no question
Only in fingerspelled names
Never — it should always be avoided in favor of simple order
practice.explain: Topic-comment order helps signal new information, contrast, or reference to earlier context; short, obvious sentences don't require it.

lessons.title: Pronouns and Using Space
lessons.intro: ASL does not have separate signs for 'he,' 'she,' 'him,' or 'her' the way English does — instead it points to locations in the space around the signer, and mastering this spatial referencing system is what lets a conversation about several people stay clear without constant repetition of names.

sections.heading: Pointing as Pronouns
body: A simple index-finger point toward a person present in the room functions as a third-person pronoun ('he/she/they'), and pointing to yourself means 'I/me,' while pointing outward toward the addressee means 'you.' Unlike spoken English pronouns, ASL pronoun points do not encode gender at all — the same point can mean 'he,' 'she,' or 'they' depending entirely on who or what location it refers to.

This is efficient in face-to-face conversation about people who are physically present, but it raises an obvious question for people who are not in the room: how do you point to someone who isn't there? The answer is spatial referencing, sometimes called setting up space, covered next.

sections.heading: Setting Up Space for Absent People
body: To talk about someone who is not physically present, a signer first names them (fingerspelling or signing their name) and then assigns them an imaginary location in the space in front of the signer — a small point or brief glance toward, say, the signer's upper-left area. From then on in the conversation, pointing to that same upper-left spot refers back to that specific person, without needing to repeat their name.

This same spatial system extends to directional verbs, which move between established locations to show who is doing what to whom: a verb like GIVE can move from the space assigned to person A toward the space assigned to person B to mean 'A gives to B,' reversing direction to mean 'B gives to A' — the verb's movement itself carries subject-object information that English would need separate words for. Keeping your spatial assignments consistent throughout a conversation is essential; reusing a location for a different person without resetting it will genuinely confuse a fluent ASL conversation partner.

example.problem: You are describing a conversation between two absent friends, Kai and Noa, and want to sign 'Kai gave the book to Noa.' Describe the spatial steps.
steps: Establish Kai's location: fingerspell/sign KAI, then point to or glance toward a spot, for example the signer's left.
Establish Noa's location: fingerspell/sign NOA, then point to or glance toward a different spot, for example the signer's right.
Sign BOOK, then use the directional verb GIVE, moving it from Kai's established left location toward Noa's established right location to show the direction of the giving.
example.answer: Set up KAI on the left and NOA on the right, then sign BOOK GIVE moving the verb from left to right, showing Kai gave the book to Noa.

keyTerms.def: An index-finger point toward a person or established location, functioning as 'I,' 'you,' 'he/she,' or 'they' with no gender marking.
Assigning an absent person a specific location in the signing space so later points and verbs can refer back to them.
A verb that physically moves between established spatial locations to show who is doing what to whom.

practice.q: Does a single ASL pronoun point encode gender the way English 'he' or 'she' does?
choices: No — the same point can mean he, she, or they depending on the referent
Yes — pointing with the left hand always means 'she'
Yes — a raised pinky always marks 'he'
ASL has no pronouns at all
practice.explain: ASL pronoun points are not gender-marked; the same physical point refers to whichever person or location has been established, regardless of gender.

practice.q: How does a signer refer to someone who is not physically present?
choices: By naming them once and assigning them a specific spot in the signing space to point back to
By fingerspelling their full name every single time they are mentioned
It is grammatically impossible in ASL to discuss absent people
By always pointing directly at the addressee instead
practice.explain: Setting up space lets a signer name someone once, assign them a location, and refer back to that location without repeating the name.

practice.q: What does a directional verb like GIVE show by moving from one established location to another?
choices: Who is doing the action and who is receiving it
The tense of the sentence (past, present, future)
Whether the sentence is a question
The gender of the people involved
practice.explain: Directional verbs move between spatially established referents to show subject-to-object direction, doing grammatical work English handles with separate words.

units.title: Everyday Vocabulary and Description
units.summary: The final unit adds family, time, and calendar vocabulary, then introduces classifiers, the powerful ASL tool for describing size, shape, and movement.

lessons.title: Family Signs
lessons.intro: Family vocabulary is some of the most frequently used signing in daily life, and ASL builds most of its family signs from a small set of reused handshapes and locations, which makes the whole category faster to learn than it first appears.

sections.heading: Core Family Signs
body: MOTHER is commonly signed with a '5' handshape (all fingers spread), thumb tapping the chin, and FATHER uses the same handshape and tapping motion but at the forehead — the paired locations (lower on the face for the female-associated sign, higher for the male-associated sign) recur across several ASL family signs, including GRANDMOTHER and GRANDFATHER, which use a similar handshape with an outward arcing double-motion at the chin or forehead respectively.

SISTER and BROTHER share a related pattern: many signers form these starting from a handshape near the forehead, then bringing both hands together in front of the body to a shared 'same' location, reflecting the sibling relationship as two people linked at the same generational point. Because regional and generational variation is common in family signs, a Deaf person's family signs learned from their own family sometimes differ slightly from a textbook version, and adapting to the specific Deaf community you interact with is normal and expected.

sections.heading: Extended Family and Talking About Your Own
body: PARENTS is often signed by combining or alternating the MOTHER and FATHER handshapes and locations, and CHILD uses a distinct patting motion at about the height of a small child, extended sideways with a sweeping repetition to indicate the plural CHILDREN. COUSIN typically uses a fingerspelled 'C' handshape shaken slightly near the side of the head, one of several family-related signs that draws on fingerspelling's initial-letter convention rather than an iconic gesture.

To describe your own family, combine these signs with the possessive point MY and the topic-comment order from Unit 3: MY MOTHER, NAME [fingerspelled name] introduces a specific family member by first establishing the relationship (topic) and then giving further detail (comment), exactly the same sentence-building pattern used for any other topic.

example.problem: Using topic-comment order, introduce your grandmother by name, given GRANDMOTHER, MY, and NAME as available signs.
steps: Establish the topic: MY GRANDMOTHER, with the topic-marking raised eyebrows and pause from Unit 3.
Comment with additional information: NAME, followed by her fingerspelled name.
example.answer: MY GRANDMOTHER, NAME [fingerspelled name] — topic (grandmother) established first, then the comment giving her name.

keyTerms.def: Signed with a similar '5' handshape tapping the chin (MOTHER) or forehead (FATHER).
A recurring ASL pattern where female-associated signs use a lower facial location and male-associated signs use a higher one.

practice.q: What is the main handshape/location difference between MOTHER and FATHER?
choices: Same handshape, tapping the chin for MOTHER versus the forehead for FATHER
Completely different handshapes with no relationship
MOTHER uses one hand, FATHER uses two hands
They are signed identically with no distinction
practice.explain: MOTHER and FATHER share a handshape but differ in location, chin versus forehead, a pattern repeated in related family signs.

practice.q: Why might a Deaf person's personal family signs differ slightly from a textbook version?
choices: Regional and family variation is common and normal in ASL vocabulary
Textbooks are always wrong about ASL
Family signs are not real ASL signs
Only hearing signers use standardized family signs
practice.explain: Like any living language, ASL has regional and family-level variation, so adapting to a specific Deaf community's usage is expected.

practice.q: How would you begin a topic-comment sentence introducing your own mother?
choices: MY MOTHER (topic, with raised eyebrows and a pause), then comment
NAME MY MOTHER WHAT (as a question only)
MOTHER alone, with no possessive or topic marking
Fingerspelling M-O-T-H-E-R every time instead of signing MOTHER
practice.explain: Following topic-comment structure, MY MOTHER is established as the topic first, then followed by a comment such as her name.

lessons.title: Time and Calendar Signs
lessons.intro: ASL treats time spatially, mapping past, present, and future onto physical space around the body, so before memorizing individual day and month signs it helps to understand the timeline itself.

sections.heading: The ASL Time Line
body: ASL commonly maps time onto an imaginary line running through the signer's body: signs near or touching the body typically represent the present or near-present, signing motion backward over the shoulder represents the past, and signing motion forward, away from the body, represents the future. TODAY is signed close to the body with a short double-tap motion, YESTERDAY moves back over the shoulder, and TOMORROW moves forward and slightly up from the cheek.

This spatial timeline is reused constantly: LAST-WEEK and NEXT-WEEK use the WEEK sign (typically one flat hand's index finger sliding along the other hand's palm) with the whole sign moved backward or forward along the same timeline, rather than requiring an entirely separate vocabulary word the way English does with 'last' and 'next.'

sections.heading: Days, Time of Day, and Clock Time
body: Many day-of-week signs use a fingerspelled initial letter with a small circular motion — such as a 'W' handshape circling for WEDNESDAY — reusing the fingerspelling-initial convention introduced earlier for signs like COUSIN. Morning, afternoon, evening, and night each have their own iconic signs roughly tracing the sun's position: MORNING mimics the sun rising over one arm, and NIGHT often uses a downward, closing motion evoking darkness falling.

Clock time is expressed by combining a number handshape with the sign HOUR, and adding MINUTE or a specific number for minutes past the hour. As with age in Unit 2, once TIME or HOUR establishes the topic, later numbers alone are often enough to communicate the specific time without repeating the whole phrase.

example.problem: Using the ASL timeline concept, explain how a signer would show 'next month' differs in space from 'last month,' assuming both use the sign MONTH.
steps: MONTH alone is a neutral sign with no inherent time direction.
To mean 'next month,' the sign MONTH moves forward, away from the body, along the established future direction of the ASL timeline.
To mean 'last month,' the sign MONTH instead moves backward, toward or over the shoulder, along the established past direction.
example.answer: NEXT-MONTH moves the MONTH sign forward (future direction); LAST-MONTH moves it backward toward the shoulder (past direction) — same base sign, opposite spatial direction.

keyTerms.def: A spatial convention where signs near the body mark the present, backward motion marks the past, and forward motion marks the future.
Several day-of-week signs that use a fingerspelled initial letter combined with a small circular motion.

practice.q: On the ASL spatial timeline, which direction typically represents the future?
choices: Forward, away from the body
Backward, over the shoulder
Straight up above the head
Time has no spatial direction in ASL
practice.explain: ASL commonly signs future events with forward motion away from the body, and past events with backward motion over the shoulder.

practice.q: How does YESTERDAY typically differ in signing direction from TOMORROW?
choices: YESTERDAY moves backward over the shoulder; TOMORROW moves forward from the cheek
They are signed with an identical forward motion
YESTERDAY uses two hands, TOMORROW uses one
Both signs are identical to TODAY
practice.explain: YESTERDAY moves backward along the past direction of the timeline; TOMORROW moves forward along the future direction, opposite spatial motions.

practice.q: What convention do many day-of-week signs (like WEDNESDAY) rely on?
choices: A fingerspelled initial letter combined with a small circular motion
A completely arbitrary handshape with no connection to the letter
The same handshape used for all seven days
A point toward a physical calendar
practice.explain: Several day signs reuse the fingerspelling-initial convention, such as a 'W' handshape circling for Wednesday.

lessons.title: Classifiers: Describing Size, Shape, and Movement
lessons.intro: Classifiers are one of the most powerful and distinctly visual tools in ASL grammar — handshapes that stand in for whole categories of objects, letting a signer show exactly how something moved, where it sat, or what shape it had, often more precisely than a spoken sentence easily could.

sections.heading: What a Classifier Is
body: A classifier is a handshape that represents a category or class of object rather than a specific fixed vocabulary sign — for instance, an upright index finger commonly stands in for a person standing or walking, and a flat, extended hand commonly represents flat surfaces or vehicles. Once a classifier has been introduced by first naming the actual object (CAR, then switching to the vehicle classifier handshape), the classifier can move through space to show exactly how that object moved, positioned, or interacted with something else.

This lets a signer show, for example, a car swerving around another car, or a person walking up to and then past a building, using the classifier's movement path itself to convey the spatial event, information that a spoken English sentence would need several extra words and phrases to convey with comparable precision.

sections.heading: Using Classifiers to Describe a Scene
body: To describe 'the cup is on the table,' a signer would first establish TABLE (perhaps with a flat classifier representing the tabletop surface), then introduce CUP, then use a classifier handshape representing a small cylindrical object placed on top of the established table location, the placement itself, not a separate word for 'on,' conveying the spatial relationship.

Classifiers are also used to describe size and shape directly: tracing the outline of a round object with both hands moving apart in a curve conveys roundness and approximate size in a single fluid motion, without needing a separate adjective sign for 'round' plus another for the specific measurement. This is one of the clearest examples of how ASL's visual-spatial grammar can pack information into a single classifier construction that a linear, word-by-word spoken sentence has to build up piece by piece.

example.problem: Describe, step by step, how a signer would show 'the ball rolled off the table and under the chair' using classifiers.
steps: Establish TABLE with its classifier location, then establish CHAIR at a nearby but distinct location.
Introduce BALL, then switch to a rounded classifier handshape representing the ball.

Move the ball classifier from the established table location, off its edge, and along a path ending underneath the established chair location, the path and endpoint of the movement itself conveying 'rolled off... and under...' without separate signs for each preposition.
example.answer: Establish TABLE and CHAIR as distinct locations, then move a rounded classifier handshape (representing the ball) from the table's edge to underneath the chair's location, with the movement path itself conveying 'rolled off and under.'

keyTerms.def: A handshape representing a category of object (person, vehicle, flat surface, small round object) used to show movement, position, or shape spatially.
The required step of first naming an object with its regular sign before switching to its classifier handshape to describe its movement or position.

practice.q: What must a signer do before using a classifier handshape to describe an object's movement?
choices: First name the object with its regular sign
Nothing — classifiers can be used with no prior context
Fingerspell the object's name three times
Use the classifier only for people, never for objects
practice.explain: A classifier must be introduced by first naming the actual object so the audience knows what the classifier handshape is standing in for.

practice.q: How does ASL typically show that 'the cup is on the table' using classifiers, rather than a separate word for 'on'?
choices: By physically placing the cup classifier on top of the established table classifier location
By fingerspelling the word O-N
By repeating the sign TABLE twice
By using a completely unrelated facial expression
practice.explain: The spatial placement of one classifier relative to another conveys the relationship ('on'), rather than a separate preposition sign.

practice.q: What advantage do classifiers offer for describing a scene compared to a word-by-word spoken sentence?
choices: They can convey path, position, and shape simultaneously through a single spatial movement
They eliminate the need to ever name objects
They only work for describing people, not objects
They require no prior vocabulary at all
practice.explain: A classifier's movement path can pack spatial information (direction, position, shape) into one fluid gesture that a spoken sentence often needs multiple separate words to build up.
